Blue represented the seas around Italy
The first sponsor chose its company colour
questions.note: The team first wore blue in 1911, when Italy was a monarchy. The colour remained after the monarchy ended.

questions.question: Before becoming Ferrari’s emblem, the prancing horse was painted on what?
questions.note: It belonged to the Italian aviator Francesco Baracca, whose family encouraged Enzo Ferrari to use it for luck. Ferrari added a yellow background associated with Modena.

questions.question: The famous theme of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly evokes which animal sound?
questions.note: Ennio Morricone used a call-like motif and different timbres for the central characters. Flute, ocarina and voices helped build the western’s sound world.

questions.question: At the 1960 Rome Olympics, Ethiopia’s Abebe Bikila won the marathon with an unusual choice of footwear. What did he wear?
questions.note: Bikila ran through Rome barefoot and won Olympic gold. A city associated with ancient monuments became the setting for one of modern distance running’s defining images.

questions.question: Italy’s Sanremo song festival helped inspire which international competition?
questions.note: The televised festival offered a model for a song competition shared across borders. The first Eurovision contest followed in 1956 in Lugano, with seven countries taking part.

questions.question: Before building luxury sports cars, Ferruccio Lamborghini had made his name producing what?
questions.note: Lamborghini’s earlier business turned wartime vehicles into useful tractors. His sports-car company came later, giving a glamorous motoring name some very practical agricultural roots.

questions.question: You order sushi with vegetables or cooked seafood instead of raw fish. What still makes it sushi?
questions.note: Sushi rice is dressed with vinegar, often with sugar and salt. Raw fish is one possible accompaniment, rather than the ingredient that every version must contain.

questions.question: Ramen is now a worldwide symbol of Japanese food. Where do its noodle roots lead?
questions.note: Ramen developed in Japan from Chinese-style wheat noodles. A food can become closely identified with one country while carrying a history of travel and adaptation.

questions.question: Crisp tempura feels thoroughly Japanese, but visitors from which European country influenced its development?
questions.note: Portuguese visitors helped introduce the style of frying that developed into tempura several centuries ago. By the Edo period, it was being sold from street stalls as a quick meal. Even the little scraps of fried batter have a use, becoming crunchy additions to noodle dishes.

questions.question: The name oyakodon means “parent-and-child bowl.” Which ingredients explain it?
questions.note: The parent is the chicken and the child is the egg, served together over rice. The name turns an ordinary combination into a small family joke.

questions.question: A successful 1970s campaign helped turn which takeaway into a Christmas tradition for many people in Japan?
questions.note: KFC launched its “Kentucky for Christmas” campaign in Japan in 1974. The promotion grew into a seasonal custom—a reminder that traditions can begin in an advertising department.

questions.question: Beans do not have to be savoury. What is the classic filling in Japan’s dorayaki, a pair of small pancakes?
questions.note: Azuki beans are cooked into a sweet paste and sandwiched between two small pancakes. Beans can play a dessert role as comfortably as a savoury one.

questions.question: Japanese curry has Indian roots, but through which country did it reach Japan in the nineteenth century?
questions.note: Curry reached Japan through Britain, which had already adapted dishes from India. Its journey did not simply go straight from one neighbouring Asian cuisine to another.

questions.question: What did instant-noodle inventor Momofuku Ando see American buyers do that helped inspire Cup Noodles?
choices: Prepare and eat the noodles in cups
Toast the dry noodles like breakfast cereal
Wrap the noodles in bread to make sandwiches
Blend the noodles into a drink
questions.note: The buyers broke noodles into cups, added hot water and ate them with forks. Ando saw that changing the container could help his Japanese invention fit a different way of eating.

questions.question: When you drink matcha, what happens to the green tea leaves?
choices: You drink them as a fine powder mixed into the water
They are strained out after a very long steep
They are squeezed for juice and then discarded
questions.note: Matcha is finely powdered green tea whisked into water. A bamboo whisk helps blend the powder instead of removing it as spent leaves.

questions.question: A perfect bowl of noodles sits in a Japanese restaurant window all day without changing. What is it likely to be?
choices: A real meal kept frozen behind the glass
A dish coated in edible preserving jelly
A real meal replaced every few minutes
questions.note: Many restaurants display remarkably lifelike models of their dishes. The models turn a menu into something you can see before ordering, without needing to know the name of every dish.

questions.question: A museum calls its subject “Edo-Tokyo”. What is the relationship between those two names?
choices: They name the same city at different times
They are two cities joined into one capital
One names the city and the other its river
One is the city’s name and the other its ruling family
questions.note: Edo was renamed Tokyo in 1868 as Japan entered a new political era. The museum’s name lets you travel through the history of one city, from the shoguns’ seat to the modern capital.

questions.question: The word “geisha” literally points to an “arts person”. What is central to the profession?
choices: Caring for a shrine and conducting its rites
questions.note: Geisha train in traditional performing arts and the skills of hosting guests. Their striking appearance is only the visible part of a profession built on years of artistic practice.

questions.question: Deer roam freely around Nara’s famous shrine and park. What belief helped give them this special status?
choices: They are regarded as divine messengers
They are believed to be the emperor’s ancestors
They are thought to predict the rice harvest
They traditionally guide pilgrims to mountain summits
questions.note: The deer’s religious association helps explain their protected place in the city. Visitors now know them for roaming the park and approaching people with deer crackers.

questions.question: Engineers looked to a diving kingfisher when redesigning a Japanese bullet train’s nose. What were they trying to reduce?
choices: The boom produced when trains pass through tunnels
The glare of headlights reflected from the rails
The vibration caused by passengers walking
The heat produced when the brakes engage
questions.note: A kingfisher moves from air into water with little splash. Engineer Eiji Nakatsu used that observation to help shape a train nose that handled pressure changes more quietly.

questions.question: Mount Fuji looks peaceful in postcards. Which description is geologically correct?
choices: It is still classified as an active volcano
It is an extinct volcano with no volcanic activity possible
It is a mountain formed entirely by folded rock
It is a giant pile of rock left by a glacier
questions.note: Fuji last erupted in 1707, but it is still classed as active. The long quiet interval and the familiar snow-covered silhouette can hide that volcanic identity.

questions.question: Japan’s first bullet-train line opened just before a major event brought the world’s attention to Tokyo. Which event?
questions.note: The Tokyo–Shin-Osaka service began on 1 October 1964. The new railway and the Olympics brought two lasting images of modern Japan into view together.

questions.question: Sapporo’s enormous snow festival started with six sculptures. Who made those first creations?
questions.note: Students made six snow sculptures in Odori Park in 1950. A modest local event grew into the festival associated with the city today.

questions.question: Karate’s name means “empty hand”. What does that tell you about the martial art?
choices: The body is used without a handheld weapon
Only open palms may be used
A match begins with both hands on the floor
questions.note: Karate developed in Okinawa through local traditions and Chinese influences before spreading across Japan. Its familiar name points to weaponless practice, rather than to a particular punch.

questions.question: The red gates lining Kyoto’s Fushimi Inari shrine paths carry inscriptions. What do many of them record?
choices: The names of donors and donation dates
The names of rulers buried beneath them
The names of visiting foreign dignitaries
The names of the forest’s oldest trees
questions.note: Individuals and businesses donate torii gates to the shrine. The famous paths are also a visible record of those contributions.

questions.question: Miyajima’s huge shrine gate appears to stand in the sea. What mainly keeps it upright?
choices: Bolts fixing it to a stone base
Steel cables tied to the shore
questions.note: The great torii stands under its own enormous weight rather than on pillars driven into the seabed. Stones packed into its upper beam add weight; at low tide, the water retreats from around its feet.

questions.question: Washington, D.C.’s famous cherry blossoms have a Japanese connection. What brought thousands of the trees there in 1912?
choices: A gift of friendship from Tokyo
An order from an American fruit-growing company
A shipment intended for a Japanese temple
A prize awarded at an international gardening contest
questions.note: Tokyo’s gift helped create one of Washington’s best-known spring landscapes. A familiar Japanese seasonal pleasure became a lasting part of another country’s capital.

questions.question: “Emoji” sounds as though it comes from “emotion”. What do its Japanese parts actually mean?
questions.note: The word combines e, meaning picture, with moji, meaning a written character. The resemblance to the English word “emotion” is a coincidence, even though emoji often communicate feelings.

questions.question: On Children’s Day, Japanese families fly streamers shaped like carp. What hope does the fish express?
choices: They express hopes for strength and perseverance
They ask for a plentiful fishing season
They commemorate the start of spring planting
questions.note: A legend tells of a carp overcoming a waterfall and becoming a dragon. The streamers turn that image of effort into a wish for children.

questions.question: In a Japanese seasonal ritual, families throw beans to drive out demons. What are they symbolically making room for?
choices: A new household deity chosen each year
questions.note: The ritual marks the seasonal turn before spring in the traditional calendar. A family member may wear a demon mask, making the symbolic eviction a household event.

questions.question: At the lowered entrance area of a Japanese home, what does a visitor normally do before stepping inside?
choices: Put on a coat over their clothes
Wash their hands in the entrance basin
Wait for the host to ring a bell
questions.note: The genkan separates outdoor footwear from indoor floors. The custom is especially practical where people sit or sleep close to the floor.

questions.question: The size of a traditional Japanese room is often described by counting what?
questions.note: Tatami mats are both flooring and a familiar measure of room size, though mat dimensions vary. A room described as “six mats” turns a floor covering into a unit of space.

questions.question: In many Japanese schools, who regularly takes a turn cleaning the classrooms?
questions.note: Classes divide cleaning duties among pupils, who sweep, wipe and tidy together. Looking after the shared room becomes part of the school day, rather than just something that happens after everyone leaves.

questions.question: Japan’s compact capsule hotels originally offered a practical answer to which everyday problem?
choices: Needing to quarantine after overseas travel
Finding a room large enough for a whole family
Storing luggage during a short station stop
questions.note: Early capsule hotels catered to workers needing an affordable overnight stay. A bed-sized private compartment and shared facilities turned a missed train into a manageable night away from home.

questions.question: A Japanese daruma goal-setting doll often starts with only one painted eye. When is the second eye filled in?
questions.note: The unpainted eye keeps an unfinished ambition visible. When the goal is achieved, completing the face turns private progress into a little ceremony.

questions.question: The little cat with a raised paw often seen in Japanese shops can look as though it is waving goodbye. What is it actually doing?
questions.note: The maneki-neko is beckoning, welcoming customers or good fortune. The same hand movement can look different to someone used to beckoning with the palm facing upwards.

questions.question: The Tale of Genji was written about a thousand years ago. Who created this landmark of Japanese literature?
choices: A woman serving at the imperial court
A Buddhist monk writing in a monastery
A warrior recording life in a castle
questions.note: The writer is known as Murasaki Shikibu, a woman at the imperial court. A major work of Japanese literature came from her observation of courtly life, centuries before the modern novel.

questions.question: Look past the enormous wave in Hokusai’s famous print: which Japanese landmark appears small in the distance?
questions.note: The wave dominates the image, but Fuji is part of its composition. The print belongs to Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji and uses the imported pigment Prussian blue.

questions.question: How can an actor in Japanese Noh theatre make a rigid mask seem to change expression?
choices: By changing its angle and the way they move
By inflating small air pockets behind its cheeks
By pulling strings attached to its eyebrows
By changing its colour with body heat
questions.note: Small changes in a mask’s angle can change how its expression is perceived. Noh brings mask, movement, voice and music together.

questions.question: An English edition of a Japanese manga seems to open at the “back”. Why might the publisher have kept it that way?
choices: To preserve the original right-to-left reading order
To separate the pictures from the dialogue
To place the ending before a long flashback
To make the book easier to hold with one hand
questions.note: Many translated manga preserve the Japanese arrangement of pages and panels. What looks backwards to an English-language reader is the original reading direction.

questions.question: Kabuki is associated with male performers, including men in female roles. Who helped begin the form?
choices: A group of samurai performing for their ruler
A religious order presenting sacred dramas
A company adapting Chinese puppet plays
questions.note: Izumo no Okuni performed in Kyoto in the early seventeenth century. Women were later banned from the public stage, changing who could perform the tradition.

questions.question: Which origami bird became a powerful symbol of hope and peace, especially through the story of Hiroshima child Sadako Sasaki?
questions.note: Sadako folded paper cranes while ill with leukaemia after surviving the atomic bombing as a young child. Cranes are still offered at the Children’s Peace Monument; she folded more than a thousand, despite a popular version saying she never reached that number.

questions.question: What keeps a bonsai tree small?
choices: Careful pruning and training of an ordinary tree
Seeds from a naturally miniature tree species
A permanently dormant stage before adulthood
A special soil that stops all new growth
questions.note: Bonsai are generally ordinary trees shaped through long-term care, including pruning roots and branches. The miniature landscape is a cultivated result, not a separate species of tiny tree.

questions.question: A broken Japanese bowl is repaired using kintsugi. What happens to its cracks?
choices: They become visible lines highlighted with gold
They are hidden under a new glaze over the whole bowl
They are covered by carving a pattern into the surface
They disappear when the clay is fired again
questions.note: Lacquer holds the fragments together and gold highlights the seams. Related repair techniques use silver or lacquer alone; in each case, repair can become part of the object’s appearance.

questions.question: A historical ninja needed to gather information without attracting attention. Which outfit would fit that job?
choices: The clothes of an ordinary travelling merchant
A distinctive black uniform worn in every situation
A warrior’s armour displaying their employer’s crest
Ceremonial robes identifying them as a royal messenger
questions.note: Ninja manuals describe disguises such as merchants, priests and performers. Looking like someone with an ordinary reason to travel could be more useful than looking like the ninja of a film.

questions.question: Japanese art helped reshape Van Gogh’s painting. How did he get to know its visual world?
choices: Through Japanese prints imported into Europe
During a long painting trip through Japan
Through training at a Japanese art school
By sharing a studio with Japanese printmakers in Arles
questions.note: Japanese woodblock prints helped change his use of colour and composition. His idea of Japan was partly an imagined one, formed through pictures rather than a visit.

questions.question: According to Pac-Man’s creator, what meal helped inspire the character’s round shape and open mouth?
choices: A pizza with a slice missing
A doughnut with a hole in the middle
A bowl of rice with chopsticks across it
A sandwich cut into two triangles
questions.note: Toru Iwatani described seeing the shape in a partly eaten pizza. A game about eating acquired a hero whose silhouette could itself be found on a dinner plate.

questions.question: The original Godzilla reached cinemas in 1954. Which anxiety helped shape its destructive monster?
choices: The possibility of invasion from space
questions.note: The black-and-white film was made after nuclear war and amid hydrogen-bomb testing in the Pacific. Its monster story carried fears that were very close to contemporary life.

questions.question: What did Nintendo originally make when it was founded in 1889?
questions.note: Nintendo began in Kyoto making hanafuda playing cards in 1889. Its business was already games, but its first players did not need a screen.

questions.question: Which childhood pastime helped inspire Pokémon’s creator to make a game about finding and collecting creatures?
questions.note: Satoshi Tajiri grew up exploring ponds and fields around his home. As those places disappeared under development, Pokémon offered children another world in which to discover and collect creatures.

questions.question: Hello Kitty is a Japanese creation. In Sanrio’s fictional biography, where was she born?
questions.note: Sanrio places Kitty White’s birth in suburban London. The global icon’s invented biography is British, even though the company that created her is Japanese.

questions.question: Why did the original Mario get such a prominent moustache and a hat?
choices: They made his face readable with very few pixels
They copied the appearance of the designer’s father
They matched the uniform of a company sponsoring the game
They identified him as a villain in the original story
questions.note: Designer Shigeru Miyamoto explained that the moustache saved the need to draw a mouth, while the hat simplified the hair. Technical limits helped create one of the most recognisable faces in games.

questions.question: Before a sumo bout, a wrestler may throw salt into the ring. What is the ritual meant to do?
choices: Signal a challenge to the referee
questions.note: The salt belongs to sumo’s ritual preparation and expresses a wish for safety in a purified ring. Some of the ceremony around a bout lasts longer than the wrestling itself.

questions.question: Baseball’s Japanese history began well before the post-war American occupation. Who introduced it to students in 1872?
choices: An American teacher working in Japan
A Japanese emperor returning from a tour
A touring team of Hollywood actors
A British naval officer stationed in Tokyo
questions.note: Teacher Horace Wilson introduced the game to his students in the nineteenth century. Japan’s deep baseball culture therefore has roots far older than the television era or post-war occupation.

questions.question: Judo is often translated as “the gentle way”. How can that idea make sense in a sport full of throws?
choices: Using an opponent’s force and lost balance
Avoiding all physical contact during a contest
Moving as slowly as possible before each throw
Awarding victory to whoever uses the least time
questions.note: The principle includes yielding and redirecting an opponent’s effort instead of simply opposing it. “Gentle” points to an approach to force, rather than a promise that nobody will hit the mat.

questions.question: The word karaoke combines Japanese words meaning what?
questions.note: Kara means “empty,” and oke is a shortening of okesutora, the Japanese borrowing of “orchestra.” The name describes an accompaniment that leaves room for the participant’s voice.

questions.question: Long before chocolate became a sweet bar, how did people in Mesoamerica commonly enjoy cacao?
questions.note: Cacao drinks have a long history in Mesoamerica, including what is now Mexico. Sweet chocolate bars came much later; the early drinks were quite different from today’s milky hot chocolate.

questions.question: Which fruit gives guacamole its creamy green base?
questions.note: The name comes from Nahuatl words for avocado and sauce. Early versions combined avocado with tomatoes and chillies, crushed together in a stone mortar.

questions.question: Nachos sound like a name for a snack. What does the name actually remember?
choices: The nickname of the man credited with making them
The town where the first tortillas were baked
A word meaning “crunchy” in an Indigenous language
The name of the cheese originally used
questions.note: Ignacio “Nacho” Anaya is credited with creating the dish in the Mexican border town of Piedras Negras. “Nacho’s special” became a food name that travelled far beyond the man who made it.

questions.question: The vanilla in familiar cakes and ice cream originally came from a Mexican plant. What kind of plant produces vanilla pods?
questions.note: Vanilla was cultivated in the Totonac region of Veracruz and Puebla before the Spanish arrived. It was also used to flavour cacao drinks, long before it became familiar in cakes and ice cream.

questions.question: In Mexico, chocolate can turn up in mole, a sauce served with meat. What does that tell you about chocolate?
choices: It can be an ingredient in savoury cooking
It must always be sweetened before use
It can only be used in cold sauces
It replaces every spice in a sauce
questions.note: Some moles combine chocolate with chillies, seeds and other ingredients to make a savoury sauce. Mole is a whole family of sauces, and many versions contain no chocolate.

questions.question: A chilli pepper can make a person’s mouth burn. Which animal can eat it without that same fiery sensation?
questions.note: Birds do not react to the pepper’s capsaicin the way mammals do. They can eat the fruits and spread the seeds—a useful partnership behind an ingredient so familiar in Mexican cooking.

questions.question: The domestic turkeys raised for meals today trace their ancestry to birds domesticated in which place?
questions.note: The modern domestic turkey descends from birds domesticated in Mexico. Some travelled to Europe and later back across the Atlantic, giving a familiar festive meal a surprisingly roundabout history.

questions.question: Caesar salad sounds as though it belongs to ancient Rome. Which city is associated with its creation?
questions.note: The best-known account credits Italian immigrant Caesar Cardini’s restaurant in Tijuana. The exact inventor and circumstances are disputed, but the name is not a tribute to Julius Caesar.

questions.question: Tequila comes from a spiky plant that can look like a cactus. What is the plant actually called?
questions.note: Tequila is made from agave, not from a cactus. The plant-shaped landscape around Tequila is so closely tied to the drink’s history that UNESCO recognises the fields and old distilleries together.

questions.question: A rotating stack of meat in a Mexican taco shop can look familiar to someone who knows shawarma. Which migrants helped create that connection?
questions.note: Lebanese migrants brought a cooking tradition that was adapted into one of Mexico City’s signature street foods. The rotating meat stack remained, while locally seasoned pork and corn tortillas made the dish distinct.

questions.question: If you could look beneath central Mexico City, what earlier city would you find traces of?
choices: An Indigenous capital built before the Spanish conquest
A colonial port abandoned when its harbour dried up
A Spanish mining settlement destroyed by an earthquake
A royal resort built for a visiting French emperor
questions.note: The Spanish built their city over Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital. At nearby Xochimilco, canals and artificial islands preserve another part of the valley’s older landscape.

questions.question: The pyramid at Chichén Itzá is one of Mexico’s most familiar images. Which civilisation built this city?
questions.note: Chichén Itzá was a Maya city, with buildings that also show influences from central Mexico. Mexico’s ancient monuments belong to different peoples and periods, rather than to one single civilisation.

questions.question: Parts of Mexico City are slowly sinking. What human activity is a major cause?
choices: Pumping water from beneath the old lakebed
Mining away salt deposits under the streets
The weight of buildings bending solid bedrock
Deep subway tunnels draining the surface canals
questions.note: Removing groundwater causes the soft ground under the city to compact. The modern capital still lives with the consequences of being built on an ancient lakebed.

questions.question: Yucatán’s cenotes are natural pools that can open into caves. What process made these inviting swimming holes?
choices: An extinct volcanic crater filling with rain
A river cutting off one of its bends
Sea waves enclosing a coastal lagoon
questions.note: Rainwater dissolves limestone and opens underground cavities. Where a cave roof collapses, the water is exposed; cenotes were important water sources for Maya communities.

questions.question: Which insects gather in such numbers in central Mexico’s mountain forests that their weight can bend branches?
questions.note: Monarch butterflies spend the winter clustered in these mountain forests. Their annual migration cycle spans several generations, so the whole round trip is larger than one butterfly’s lifetime.

questions.question: The axolotl, a Mexican salamander often seen as a smiling little creature, has a remarkable ability. What can it do after losing a leg?
choices: Heal the wound but keep a stump
Replace the leg with a smaller fin
Grow a new limb only before adulthood
questions.note: This Mexican salamander can rebuild a functional limb, which makes it valuable to regeneration research. It also keeps external gills into adulthood and normally remains in the water.

questions.question: Why do grey whales travel to the sheltered lagoons of Baja California in winter?
choices: Rest through winter without eating or moving
questions.note: The lagoons of Ojo de Liebre and San Ignacio are important breeding grounds within El Vizcaíno. Mexico’s desert coast is also a nursery for these ocean travellers.

questions.question: Before it became a US state, California was part of which country?
questions.note: California passed from Mexico to the United States under the treaty that ended the Mexican-American War in 1848. The border moved, leaving a Mexican chapter inside what is now familiar American geography.

questions.question: Buried beneath part of Mexico’s Yucatán region is evidence of which event that changed life on Earth?
choices: The asteroid impact linked to the dinosaurs’ mass extinction
A volcanic eruption that began the last ice age
The earthquake that opened the Atlantic Ocean
The crater left by the largest eruption in human history
questions.note: The enormous Chicxulub impact crater dates to about 66 million years ago. The impact and its aftermath helped wipe out the non-avian dinosaurs, connecting a Mexican landscape to a global turning point.

questions.question: Mexico City’s Xochimilco canals run between artificial islands. What was their practical purpose before they became a famous visitor attraction?
questions.note: These human-made farming plots occupy a landscape of canals and lake areas. They are part of a food-growing tradition that UNESCO includes in its account of Mexican cuisine.

questions.question: Day of the Dead can look like a festival of skeletons. What is at the heart of it?
choices: Remembering relatives and loved ones who have died
Marking the beginning of the new year
Welcoming the first rains of spring
questions.note: Families may prepare an ofrenda with photographs and foods associated with the people they remember. Practices vary between communities, bringing personal memories into a shared annual celebration.

questions.question: Why do families traditionally lay trails of marigolds for Día de los Muertos?
choices: To guide loved ones’ spirits home
To show the route of the children’s procession
To mark houses hosting wedding guests
To symbolise the boundary of a private garden
questions.note: In the tradition, the flowers’ colour and scent help the dead find their way to the ofrenda. Photographs and favourite foods make that welcome personal.

questions.question: Mexico City launched a spectacular new Day of the Dead parade in 2016. What helped inspire its format?
choices: A parade staged for a James Bond film
A newly discovered Aztec festival manual
An old painting showing the same annual route
A royal procession preserved from colonial times
questions.note: Spectre opened with a fictional parade filmed in Mexico City, and a real parade followed. The film influenced this particular public event, not the much older Day of the Dead traditions themselves.

questions.question: Under its colourful paper, what traditionally formed the breakable body of a Mexican Christmas piñata?
questions.note: The traditional piñata covered an earthenware pot with bright paper and filled it with treats. The decorated container was meant to be broken so its fruit and sweets could fall to the waiting group.

questions.question: Before Christmas, groups in Mexico go from door to door in Las Posadas. Whose search for shelter are they acting out?
questions.note: The celebrations recall Mary and Joseph’s search for lodging. In Mexico they run from 16 to 24 December, often joining a procession with food and a piñata.

questions.question: Cinco de Mayo is often marketed abroad as Mexico’s Independence Day. What does it actually commemorate?
choices: A Mexican victory over French troops
The end of Spanish colonial rule
The adoption of the current national flag
The signing of a peace treaty with the United States
questions.note: The date remembers the Battle of Puebla in 1862. Mexico’s Independence Day is in September, so the two celebrations recall different struggles.

questions.question: In the nineteenth century, Mexico briefly had an emperor born in Vienna. What was his background?
choices: A Mexican general educated in Austria
A French merchant elected by parliament
questions.note: Maximilian accepted Mexico’s crown with French support and the backing of Mexican conservatives. His story connects Mexican political conflict with the dynastic ambitions of Europe.

questions.question: Mexico’s flag shows an eagle, a cactus and a snake. The emblem points back to the story of what?
choices: The founding of the city beneath Mexico City
The first Spanish landing on the coast
The discovery of Mexico’s largest silver mine
The signing of the independence declaration
questions.note: The emblem draws on the founding legend of Tenochtitlan. Its familiar modern form developed through different historical versions; it is more than a collection of national wildlife.

questions.question: A Mexican game called lotería plays a little like bingo. What do players match on their boards instead of numbers?
questions.note: A caller announces a card and players cover its matching picture. Dried beans can serve as markers, bringing a kitchen staple onto the game board.

questions.question: In Mexico’s Voladores ceremony, four performers circle down through the air on ropes. What are they descending from?
questions.note: A musician remains at the top, playing a flute and small drum. The ceremony is especially associated with Totonac communities and expresses a relationship with the natural and spiritual worlds.

questions.question: Frida Kahlo painted while confined to bed after an accident. What was fitted above the bed to help her see her subject?
questions.note: Her mother had a mirror installed on the four-poster bed. It made her own face available as a subject; the bed and mirror can be seen at the Casa Azul museum.

questions.question: Diego Rivera painted a mural for New York’s Rockefeller Center, but it was later destroyed. What was at the centre of the dispute?
choices: He included a portrait of Lenin and refused to remove it
He used paint that was forbidden inside tall buildings
He painted over a historic mural without permission
He refused to add the building’s name in larger letters
questions.note: Rivera’s patrons objected to the communist leader’s portrait in Man at the Crossroads. The conflict ended with the mural covered and then removed from the wall—a commission that became a clash over who controlled its message.

questions.question: Mexico’s colourful alebrijes can combine wings, horns and body parts from different animals. What are these figures?
choices: Portraits of a single ancient royal family
Scientific models used in biology classes
questions.note: Pedro Linares developed these figures in Mexico City using cartonería, a paper-and-paste craft. In his account, the strange creatures came from a dream during an illness. His family continued the practice.

questions.question: The elegant Mexican skeleton in a fancy hat became an icon. What did the original image behind La Catrina poke fun at?
choices: Doctors who refused to treat the poor
Actors who forgot their lines on stage
questions.note: Printmaker José Guadalupe Posada used skeletons for social satire, including mockery of elites adopting European fashions. The grand hat makes status look ridiculous when its wearer is reduced to bones.

questions.question: Chemicals extracted from a Mexican wild yam helped pave the way for which major medicine?
questions.note: Chemicals from Mexican yams provided material for producing steroid hormones more affordably. Further research in Mexico helped lead to the oral contraceptive pill; the plant was a starting material, not a ready-made medicine.

questions.question: Sor Juana, a seventeenth-century Mexican writer who defended women’s learning, built her intellectual life in which setting?
questions.note: She maintained a study and library in the convent and spoke with scholars from the court and university. Her writing also argued for women’s access to learning.

questions.question: Which everyday English food word travelled through Spanish from Nahuatl, an Indigenous language of Mexico?
questions.note: Tomato comes through Spanish tomate from Nahuatl tomatl. The ingredient’s journey carried its name into other languages, leaving a Mexican linguistic connection on menus around the world.

questions.question: In the Mexican novel Like Water for Chocolate, Tita cannot freely express her feelings. What gives them a magical way out?
choices: The food she cooks affects the people who eat it
The clothes she sews change colour with her mood
The letters she hides begin speaking aloud
The flowers she grows repeat her secrets
questions.note: Laura Esquivel makes cooking carry Tita’s love, grief and desire beyond what she can say openly. A familiar idea—putting feeling into food—becomes literally powerful inside the story.

questions.question: Maya mathematicians developed a way to write “nothing” as part of their number system. Which familiar idea was that?
questions.note: Maya mathematics included zero and supported sophisticated calendar calculations. An apparent absence became something that could be written and used in a numerical system.

questions.question: A brilliant red used in dyes and pigments has long been produced in Mexico from cochineal. What is the source of that colour?
choices: A mineral found in volcanic rock
The bark of a tropical tree
questions.note: Cochineal insects live on prickly pear cacti and produce an intense red. Indigenous producers developed ways to raise them, turning something tiny into a highly valued colour.

questions.question: In a modern mariachi group, which brass instrument gives a bright sound above the guitars and violins?
questions.note: Trumpets join strings and voices in the modern mariachi sound. The music carries local histories as well as celebrations, with a repertoire in Spanish and Indigenous languages.

questions.question: Before Ritchie Valens made La Bamba a rock-and-roll hit, what was it?
choices: A traditional song from Mexico’s Veracruz region
questions.note: Valens learned the song through his Mexican-American family and transformed it with electric guitar and a rock-and-roll beat. The hit carried an older Mexican dance song into a new musical world.

questions.question: In Coco, a photograph on a family altar helps someone in the Land of the Dead return for a visit. What makes that possible in the film’s story?
choices: Someone among the living is remembering them
Their family has bought a special travel ticket
They have become a famous musician
They have been dead for exactly one year
questions.note: Pixar gives remembrance a visible role: a photograph means someone is there to receive the visitor. The film turns an act familiar from Day of the Dead observances into a rule of its imagined world.

questions.question: Mexican director Guillermo del Toro made Pinocchio with physical puppets. How did the filmmakers bring them to life on screen?
choices: Moving and photographing them a tiny step at a time
Filming marionettes moving continuously on strings
Drawing every frame over footage of live actors
Replacing every puppet with a computer-generated model
questions.note: Physical puppets are moved in small steps and photographed to create the performance. The film returns a story about a wooden puppet to a world of objects that the filmmakers could handle.

questions.question: For a Mexican lucha libre wrestler, which item can become an identity that continues into films and comic books?
questions.note: The design helps turn the wrestler into a recognisable character. El Santo carried his masked identity beyond the ring into films and comics, becoming a figure in wider popular culture.

questions.question: The cowboy is an icon of the American West. Which Mexican workers helped shape the skills behind that image?
choices: Silver miners carrying supplies by mule
questions.note: Mexican vaqueros were part of the history that shaped cowboy work and culture. The familiar film image compresses a more varied world that also included Indigenous herders and Black cattle hands.

questions.question: At Mexico’s 1986 football World Cup, what action by the crowd became famous around the world?
choices: Standing and sitting in sequence to send a wave around the stands
Jumping together while linking arms across each row
Turning their backs and bouncing after each goal
Raising coloured cards to build a giant national flag
questions.note: The tournament helped give the “Mexican wave” a global audience. The crowd became part of the spectacle, creating motion around the stadium without anyone leaving their seat’s position.

questions.question: In the Mexican dance often called the Hat Dance, a couple’s playful movements tell what kind of story?
choices: A family saying goodbye to a traveller
questions.note: The jarabe tapatío uses the interaction between a pair of dancers to suggest flirtation. The broad hat and elaborate clothes frame a recognisable human story, even if you have never learned the steps.

questions.question: Why did the football used at the 1970 World Cup in Mexico have such a striking black-and-white pattern?
choices: To stand out on black-and-white television
To help referees see which way it was spinning
To disguise the seams between the leather panels
To keep the ball cooler under the Mexican sun
questions.note: The Telstar’s contrasting panels helped viewers follow the ball on television. That practical design became the football many people picture when they hear the word.

questions.question: At the Mexico City Olympics, Dick Fosbury surprised viewers by clearing the high-jump bar in which way?
choices: He went over the bar backwards
He took off from both feet together
He carried a short pole for balance
He landed standing on his feet
questions.note: Fosbury cleared the bar with his back facing it and landed on the mat. His 2.24-metre winning jump helped turn an unconventional technique into the familiar style of the event.

questions.question: After Turkish coffee, the cup is sometimes turned upside down on its saucer. What is traditionally read for a fortune?
choices: Shapes left by the coffee grounds
Cracks appearing in the empty cup
The order in which sugar cubes dissolve
The colour of the accompanying water
questions.note: Turkish coffee is served with its fine grounds still in the cup. Reading the shapes they leave is one of the social customs around the drink.

questions.question: On a Turkish fish stall, palamut and torik can sound like different species. What is the main distinction?
choices: Different sizes of the same fish
One is freshwater and one is marine
One is smoked and one is pickled
Different fish caught in the same net
questions.note: Turkish fish names distinguish several growth stages of bonito. A large one called torik is used for lakerda, the salt-cured preparation.

questions.question: Turkish delight has a soft, yielding texture. What thickens the traditional sugar mixture?
questions.note: Sugar syrup and starch are cooked together, then flavoured and cut into pieces. The familiar soft block does not depend on the gelatine used in many other sweets.

questions.question: Before baking, simit is dipped in diluted molasses and coated in sesame. What does the dip help do?
choices: Hold the seeds and darken the crust
Make the bread rise without yeast
Stop the crust forming in the oven
questions.note: The syrup helps sesame cling to the dough and colours the surface as it bakes. A familiar street snack carries a small practical technique.

questions.question: The saying that forty Kayseri dumplings should fit on a spoon praises what?
choices: The cook’s skill at making them tiny
The diner’s ability to eat quickly
The amount of meat in every parcel
The size of the spoon used for serving
questions.note: The number celebrates delicate handwork rather than setting a rule for every portion. The little parcels are commonly served with garlic yogurt and pepper-coloured butter.

questions.question: Türkiye’s tea fields are concentrated around Rize. Which landscape suits them?
choices: A wet coast with steep green slopes
An arid plateau with salt flats
A Mediterranean plain with dry summers
A snowy interior with little rainfall
questions.note: The eastern Black Sea coast provides the rain needed for tea growing. Large-scale cultivation developed during the twentieth century, despite tea’s now deeply familiar place in daily life.

questions.question: Turkish ice-cream sellers can stretch and lift the ice cream during their serving tricks. Which plant product helps give it that texture?
questions.note: Salep, a flour made from orchid tubers, helps thicken the milk and give Maraş ice cream its distinctive texture. That texture makes the familiar serving tricks possible.

questions.question: The dish hünkar beğendi has a name that sounds like a tiny review. What does it mean?
questions.note: The dish pairs a meat stew with a smoky aubergine purée. Its name is one example of the stories and images carried by Turkish dish names.

questions.question: Traditional tavuk göğsü is a sweet milk pudding. Which surprising ingredient gives it texture?
questions.note: The chicken is boiled, rinsed and pulled into very fine fibres. In the traditional pudding it contributes texture, challenging the expectation that meat must mean a savoury course.

questions.question: Which New York deli word is commonly traced, through Romanian and Yiddish, to Turkish pastırma?
questions.note: Etymological accounts commonly connect the words, though the Romanian word’s deeper origin is debated. The foods developed differently as the name travelled.

questions.question: Kapadokya’s “fairy chimneys” look like towers wearing stone hats. How does the harder cap help a tower survive?
choices: It shelters softer rock beneath from erosion
It lifts the softer rock as it expands
It keeps molten lava inside the column
It turns the column into solid marble
questions.note: Volcanic deposits created layers with different resistance to erosion. Soft tuff also allowed people to carve rooms and churches into the landscape.

questions.question: Pamukkale looks like a hillside of snow, even in warm weather. What makes it white?
choices: Fine salt carried inland by sea winds
Shell fragments washed up by a river
Pale volcanic ash falling each year
questions.note: Calcite-rich spring water builds the travertine terraces. The name Pamukkale means cotton castle, a visual description rather than the material it contains.

questions.question: The designers of Hagia Sophia were known for expertise in which field?
questions.note: Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus brought mathematical knowledge to the building. Its enormous dome also had an engineering history: the first collapsed and a higher replacement followed.

questions.question: What makes Göbekli Tepe’s monumental carved pillars especially surprising?
choices: They were carved with iron tools
They were built after the Egyptian pyramids
They were erected for an early farming empire
questions.note: The site belongs to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic and was built by hunter-gatherer communities. Its carved animals and large structures reveal a social world long before written records.

questions.question: At Mount Nemrut, some gods carry both Greek and Persian names. What was King Antiochus presenting through this pairing?
choices: His kingdom’s links to both traditions
A religious conversion from one to the other
A warning against the neighbouring empire
Separate monuments for rival royal families
questions.note: Commagene stood between Greek and Persian worlds. Antiochus connected his ancestry and royal monument with both.

questions.question: The word “mausoleum” comes from the monumental tomb at ancient Halicarnassus, now Bodrum. What gave the tomb its name?
choices: The stone used to build it
questions.note: Mausolus’s tomb became one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. His name later became an ordinary word for a grand tomb.

questions.question: Why do archaeologists speak of different “Troys” at the same site?
choices: New settlements were built above older ones
Several nearby towns used the same name
The inhabitants moved between seasonal camps
Different districts had independent city governments
questions.note: Troy is a layered archaeological site rather than one frozen moment from Homer. Earlier excavations sometimes damaged later layers while searching for the legendary city.

questions.question: Safranbolu’s name preserves a link with which valuable spice?
questions.note: The town lay on an important caravan route and preserves many historic houses. Its name also recalls saffron cultivation in the surrounding area.

questions.question: The pearl mullet lives in Lake Van’s alkaline water. Where does it go to spawn?
choices: Out through a river to the sea
Onto exposed mud above the lake
questions.note: Lake Van has no outlet, so dissolved minerals accumulate. The fish’s journey into streams connects a distinctive lake environment with nearby fresh water.

questions.question: A ship passing through İstanbul’s Bosphorus travels between the Black Sea and which body of water?
questions.note: Marmara in turn connects to the Aegean through the Dardanelles. These linked waterways help explain İstanbul’s strategic position.

questions.question: Before founding a steppe empire, the Göktürks were associated with making a material essential for tools and weapons. Which craft?
questions.note: Chinese accounts connect the ruling clan with ironworking for the Rouran. In 552 Bumin defeated those overlords and took the title kağan.

questions.question: Some of the earliest substantial Turkic writing survives on stone monuments far from modern Türkiye. Where?
questions.note: The eighth-century Orhun inscriptions commemorate Kül Tigin and Bilge Kağan. They place an important part of Turkic language history in Inner Asia.

questions.question: Kaşgarlı Mahmud’s medieval dictionary explained Turkic words to Arabic readers. What else did it include to help picture that world?
questions.note: The Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk included a circular map as well as vocabulary. Language learning and a view of the world appeared in the same work.

questions.question: Tulips are a symbol of the Netherlands. Through which empire’s gardening networks did bulbs reach European collectors such as Clusius?
questions.note: Tulips were prized garden plants in Ottoman lands before becoming a Dutch emblem. Clusius’s contacts helped him build the collection he brought to Leiden; he was not the first person there to grow them.

questions.question: The poet Rumi’s name points to “Rum”. What did that geographical name refer to?
choices: A river valley in northern India
A port on the Arabian coast
questions.note: Rumi settled in Konya, in the region called Rum after its Roman and Byzantine past. A poet’s familiar name preserves an older political map.

questions.question: During the 1453 siege of Constantinople, how did Ottoman ships get past a barrier across the Golden Horn?
choices: They broke the barrier with reinforced bows
They slipped past after the barrier was lowered
They crossed using a newly dug canal
questions.note: Ships were moved overland into the Golden Horn, bypassing its defensive chain. The episode is one of the siege’s most memorable engineering manoeuvres.

questions.question: Süleyman is called “the Magnificent” in Europe. Which achievement does his Turkish title Kanuni emphasise?
questions.note: Kanuni points to the laws associated with his rule. The two titles place different parts of the same reign in the foreground.

questions.question: Mimar Sinan described major mosques as his apprentice, journeyman and master works. What was he comparing his career to?
questions.note: The sequence links the Şehzade, Süleymaniye and Selimiye mosques. His description presents even monumental architecture as a craft learned over a lifetime.

questions.question: Piri Reis’s 1513 map includes notes about how it was made. What do they describe?
choices: Charting the whole coast on his own voyages
Copying one map without changing its details
questions.note: Its marginal notes identify earlier sources, including a chart associated with Columbus. The surviving map is evidence of knowledge being gathered and compared.

questions.question: Before Müteferrika’s Turkish-language press, what was already being printed in İstanbul?
choices: Books in Hebrew, Armenian and Greek
Only small images without written text
questions.note: Printing in several communities preceded the Turkish press of the 1720s. The distinction is between languages and publishing traditions, rather than printing suddenly arriving in the city.

questions.question: For Ottoman Janissaries, overturning a soup cauldron could send which message?
choices: The regiment had won a battle
A new recruit had completed training
The troops were beginning a fast
questions.note: The shared cooking vessel carried meaning beyond the meal. Upsetting it became a sign that the soldiers rejected authority.

questions.question: The Ottoman reform edict called Gülhane takes its name from a place. What kind of place was it?
questions.note: The edict was proclaimed in Topkapı’s rose garden in 1839. It announced guarantees concerning life, property and taxation, opening the Tanzimat reform period.

questions.question: Australians and New Zealanders mark Anzac Day. In Türkiye, the same 1915 campaign is remembered as Çanakkale. Which peninsula connects the names?
questions.note: The Gallipoli campaign aimed to force the straits and reach İstanbul. Its memory is shared across countries, though their names and perspectives differ.

questions.question: Türkiye’s 23 April holiday remembers the opening of its national assembly and is also dedicated to whom?
questions.note: The assembly first met in Ankara in 1920. Children’s celebrations became part of the anniversary, joining a political founding moment with a different kind of public occasion.

questions.question: İsmet, the Turkish negotiator at Lausanne, later took the surname İnönü. What did it commemorate?
choices: The town where he signed the treaty
The school where he first studied
questions.note: The surname referred to the İnönü battles. Like many names adopted after the 1934 law, it carried a personal and historical association.

questions.question: Angora appears in the names of a goat, a cat and a rabbit. What do those names point back to?
choices: A word for snowy mountain weather
A village in the Swiss Alps
questions.note: The city was known to Europeans as Angora. The name travelled widely through animals and textiles, even after Ankara became more familiar as a capital.

questions.question: Alongside political changes, the early Turkish Republic adopted international standards for which everyday matters?
choices: The names of towns, ports and mountains
The structure of meals and public holidays
The colours of flags, uniforms and stamps
questions.note: Reforms between 1925 and 1931 changed clocks, calendars and measurements. Modernisation could alter an ordinary date or quantity as well as state institutions.

questions.question: Photographs show Atatürk teaching at a blackboard in 1928. Which nationwide change was he helping introduce?
choices: A new alphabet based on Latin letters
A new spelling system using the existing script
A simplified shorthand for government clerks
A common alphabet for every regional language
questions.note: The alphabet reform changed how Turkish was written. Its 29 letters included forms chosen for Turkish sounds, making the reform a practical literacy task.

questions.question: Türkiye gave women the national vote in 1934. Which of these countries introduced it later?
questions.note: France granted women national voting rights in 1944. The comparison complicates a simple assumption that every political reform moved through countries in the same order.

questions.question: Mustafa Kemal’s surname Atatürk was not inherited. How was it given to him?
choices: By a law passed by the assembly
By a military nickname chosen in childhood
By adopting his mother’s maiden name
questions.note: The assembly granted it in November 1934, the year family surnames became compulsory. The name belongs to the history of that reform.

questions.question: The English word kiosk travelled through French from Turkish köşk. What did the Turkish word describe?
questions.note: The word moved from a garden building towards small street structures selling goods. Its modern meaning carries the shape of an older one.

questions.question: A traditional Anatolian carpet’s pile is built from knots. What does the term “symmetrical knot” describe?
choices: How yarn wraps around the foundation threads
How the visible pattern is mirrored across the centre
How the fringe is balanced at both ends
How the border repeats around the four sides
questions.note: The knot, also called the Gördes knot, wraps around two warp threads. The term describes construction rather than whether the visible pattern is symmetrical.

questions.question: Before becoming famous for a distinctive raised red, İznik pottery often used blue and white. Which imported ceramics influenced that look?
questions.note: Ottoman makers drew inspiration from Chinese porcelain while developing their own materials and designs. The later red pigment became a striking part of İznik’s identity.

questions.question: In ebru, where is the pattern made before it reaches the paper?
questions.note: The water is thickened with tragacanth so the colours float instead of sinking; they are flicked on with a horsehair brush and drawn about with a fine point. Laying paper on top lifts the pattern and destroys it in the same movement, so no two sheets can match. UNESCO listed the craft in 2014.

questions.question: Karagöz shadow theatre gets much of its comedy from the contrast between its two central characters. What is that contrast?
choices: The manners of a villager and a foreign visitor
The rivalry of an apprentice and a master
The misunderstandings of two different generations
questions.note: Karagöz and Hacivat repeatedly misunderstand one another across different ways of speaking. The translucent figures turn that verbal friction into a visual performance.

questions.question: The “whirling dervishes” are a familiar image of Türkiye. What is the Mevlevi sema in its traditional setting?
questions.note: Turning belongs to a practice involving music, discipline and religious life. Short performances for visitors do not always convey that full context.

questions.question: What does the oil add to the challenge of Turkish oil wrestling?
choices: It makes ordinary grips harder to hold
It prevents the wrestlers from bending
It marks which wrestler has scored
It fixes the leather trousers to the ground
questions.note: Wrestlers at Kırkpınar are covered in olive oil and wear leather kıspet. The slippery surface changes how opponents can secure a hold.

questions.question: In a Nasreddin Hoca story, he looks outside for a ring lost indoors. Why does he give that apparently sensible place the wrong priority?
choices: Because a neighbour told him to
Because he had already searched inside
Because his wife had locked him out
questions.note: He searches where the light is better. Versions of the joke travel across several cultures, exposing the temptation to look where searching is easy rather than where the answer might be.

questions.question: In Nuri Bilge Ceylan’s Winter Sleep, a hotel is built into which distinctive landscape?
choices: The salt flats of central Anatolia
questions.note: The 2014 Palme d’Or winner places its characters in a hotel cut into the rock. A landscape often seen in travel photographs becomes the setting for long, intimate conflicts.

questions.question: Orhan Pamuk’s Museum of Innocence exists as both a novel and a place in İstanbul. What does the museum display?
choices: Objects connected with its fictional characters
Props used in a film version of the novel
questions.note: Pamuk conceived the novel and museum together. Everyday objects create a material setting for the story and for İstanbul life in the second half of the twentieth century.

lines.text: I had no memory because memory needs an after, and there was no after.
The light should have taken me too. It did not.
The dark filled with small fires, each one a holding.
The light came from inside us. Each photon we gave to the dark was a piece of us.
Then, one afternoon, two molecules met in the water and did not let go.
The dust of dead stars shredding the dust of dead stars.
I had seen them every night of my life. I had never seen them.
A hand found my shoulder. It rested there, already at home. I touched the hand. The hand did not move away.
The face was still the face. And yet it was somewhere else.
Then I took a breath. The void blinked, made a small sound, and sat down on my blanket.
The sparrow has personally insulted him.
His heart was going so fast I could not count it, a continuous trembling like a small engine.
My tea has gone cold. I register it as a minor betrayal.
The students change, and so does the spirit of the time. The subjects don’t have to.
I had seen that movement from behind a desk. For a second, a classroom returned around him, with his coat hanging from the back of a chair and dripping onto the floor.
For a while, I called it growth.
Şafak walked out of the building into the afternoon sun, lighter than he’d been in months.
He had a perfect report card and Superman in the bag.
In the hallway at home her hand went up to unwind it anyway.
The car didn’t need me to watch anything. But my hands still hovered near the wheel.
“I’m done,” he said, testing the sentence to see how it sounded in the air.
I sat there until the stars came out. The car, parked behind me in the dark, waited for a command I no longer knew how to give.
It was ten minutes. She took twenty.
He stood at the sink, looking at the clean glass, then reached out and tightened the faucet handle, though no water was dripping.
New ideas need empty spaces to pass through.
lines.source: The Best Ideas Come When You Let Go

lines.text: We think it’s working the least when actually it’s working the hardest.
lines.source: The Best Ideas Come When You Let Go

lines.text: My friend’s life is a map. My own life is a forest.
I just need a silence that doesn’t ask questions.
Fear is not stupid. Fear is the most intelligent thing inside us.
lines.source: It Is Either from Love or Fear

lines.text: Love is the only thing I have ever done that felt like it was actually mine.
lines.source: It Is Either from Love or Fear

lines.text: A lie carries no physical weight and still expands like a black hole.
Honesty was always available. Most of us knew that.
The moment perception becomes uncomfortable is the moment it might be getting accurate.
The buildings we never question are the ones we should.
